question: How does the second étude’s detached phrasing differ from the first one’s continuous figuration?
intro: This 1920 Victor side preserves two études in sequence: “Black Keys”, then “Butterfly”. Alfred Cortot’s recorded legacy is known for flexible phrase timing, but comparisons must distinguish that documented practice from claims about an exact beat. The whole side is retained here, including the pause between the pieces.

sections.label: A′ · Black Keys return and close
sections.mNote: the opening material returns before the first étude closes

cues.title: Two tasks for the hands
cues.text: The first étude sets rapid right-hand figuration against the left hand’s harmonic support and accents. Even through the historic disc’s restricted sound, the two hands have different musical jobs: a continuous surface and a guiding foundation.
cues.evidence: Technical premise: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/gatunki/9_etiudy. The selected Victor side’s two works are identified by DAHR matrix B-23953.

cues.title: One side, two études
cues.text: Cortot recorded this pairing on 22 April 1920 in Camden, New Jersey. Victor issued the selected take on a ten-inch disc, number 64989; the second étude is part of the original side, not an addition made for this site.
cues.evidence: DAHR B-23953 take2, Camden Church Building, Victor64989: https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/matrix/detail/700009148/B-23953-Etude_in_G_flat_op._10_no._5_Black_keys

cues.title: Rubato as phrase shaping
cues.text: Cortot’s later Chopin recordings are documented as using rubato and occasional separation of the hands. That history suggests a question for this earlier side: where does the phrase seem to lean or relax? It does not establish a measured delay at this instant.
cues.evidence: Rob Challinor describes rubato and occasional hand division in Cortot’s 1942–43 recordings, not this 1920 side: https://musicwebinternational.com/2025/10/alfred-cortot-plays-chopin-apr/. Used explicitly as performer context, not a transfer of local observations.

cues.title: The first book’s dedication
cues.text: The “Black Keys” étude belongs to Op. 10, the collection Chopin dedicated to Liszt. Its keyboard restriction becomes the material of a concert piece: the pattern must still articulate phrases and harmonic direction.

cues.title: Let the first ending finish
cues.text: Listen for the first étude’s concluding gestures and decay before the next piece begins. A shared disc side does not make the two studies one uninterrupted composition.
cues.evidence: The 1:34 report boundary marks the end region. Supplementary 0.25-second RMS inspection places the final attack near 92.5 s, decay through 94.5 s and a low floor to 96.25 s. Reproducible comparison record and trim note: docs/assets/data/compare/chopin-black-keys-cortot-neeman/chopin-etude-op10-5-cortot.json .

cues.title: Another étude, another articulation
cues.text: The second piece is Op. 25 No. 9, the “Butterfly”. Its compact groups alternate connected and detached articulation, a different problem from the near-continuous right-hand stream of “Black Keys”.
cues.evidence: DAHR and Archive identify both works. The comparison record’s RMS note places renewed attacks at 96.5–96.75 s: docs/assets/data/compare/chopin-black-keys-cortot-neeman/chopin-etude-op10-5-cortot.json . Articulation design: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89tude_Op._25,_No._9_(Chopin).
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A later book of studies
cues.text: The second piece comes from Op. 25, published in 1837 and dedicated to Marie d’Agoult. The two works share G♭ major, but belong to different collections and explore different ways of touching and grouping notes.
cues.evidence: Op.25 publication/dedication: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/gatunki/9_etiudy; work identity/key in DAHR and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89tude_Op._25,_No._9_(Chopin).

cues.title: Small groups carry the melody
cues.text: In the second étude, listen for how short groups connect some notes and detach others. The melody emerges from those articulations; simply making everything equally short would erase part of the written contrast.
cues.evidence: Staccato–marcato and connected/detached alternations described in https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89tude_Op._25,_No._9_(Chopin). Passage-level explanation, not a claim about a particular Cortot attack.

transitions.title: Harmonic movement within continuous figuration
transitions.how: The first étude’s right-hand pattern continues while the harmonic direction and accents change. Listening to the left hand makes this expansion more distinct than following the fast surface alone. This is a central span within Black Keys, not the beginning of the second étude.
transitions.evidence: Report novelty at 0:28; the persisted chroma map places Neeman’s approximate 30.0-second central-region marker at 28.30 here, local similarity 0.823 and map median 0.833. Usable with caution, not bar-aligned: docs/assets/data/compare/chopin-black-keys-cortot-neeman/chopin-etude-op10-5-cortot.json .

transitions.title: The first pattern returns before its close
transitions.to: A′ · Black Keys return and close
transitions.how: The opening material returns within the first étude, keeping its rapid figuration while recovering the original harmonic orientation. The return then leads towards the final flourish. There is no change of work here; the second étude begins only after the ensuing close and pause.
transitions.evidence: The persisted chroma map places Neeman’s approximate 60.0-second return at 53.93 here, local similarity 0.905 and map median 0.833. Passage placement is usable with caution, not an exact bar boundary or measured rubato: docs/assets/data/compare/chopin-black-keys-cortot-neeman/chopin-etude-op10-5-cortot.json .

transitions.title: A completed étude, then a new attack
transitions.from: A′ · Black Keys return and close
transitions.how: Black Keys ends and its sound decays before Butterfly begins. Both pieces are in G♭ major, but the second replaces continuous right-hand figuration with compact connected-and-detached groups. The silence is a gap between independent works on one disc side, not a modulation inside a single étude.
transitions.evidence: DAHR documents the two-piece side. The persisted comparison record’s 0.25-second RMS note places the low floor at 94.5–96.25 s and renewed attacks at 96.5–96.75 s; the 1:34 report boundary marks decay, not the new opening: docs/assets/data/compare/chopin-black-keys-cortot-neeman/chopin-etude-op10-5-cortot.json .

composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: He made the piano sing through ornament, contrapuntal voice-leading and the unstable accents of Polish dance.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; Józef Elsner at Warsaw’s Main School of Music, 1826–29
Warsaw until 1830; Paris from 1831; summers at George Sand’s house in Nohant
Teaching, publication and selected performances, more often in salons than large public halls
Almost entirely centred on the piano: études, mazurkas, polonaises, nocturnes, preludes, ballades, scherzos, sonatas and concertos
composer.background:
Chopin was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810, to a French-born father, Nicolas, and a Polish mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska. The family soon moved to Warsaw, where Nicolas taught French. The name Fryderyk belongs to his Polish life; Frédéric became usual in France. His family observed his birthday on 1 March, although the baptismal record gives 22 February. Piano lessons with Wojciech Żywny introduced Bach and Mozart alongside the fashionable repertory of the day. As a child he composed polonaises and played in aristocratic houses, but his later musical education extended beyond the cultivation of a prodigy.

Józef Elsner taught him harmony and composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music from 1826 to 1829. Chopin heard Italian opera, encountered Polish vernacular music during visits outside the capital and learned the working forms of the virtuoso concerto. The F minor Concerto was composed before the E minor, despite their eventual numbering as Nos. 2 and 1. Both preserve an extended orchestral opening, but once the piano enters, its vocal line and ornament determine the movement’s scale. The slow movements belong as much to operatic singing as to the display repertory of a concert pianist.
